name: Arm Triangle from Mount
description: From mount, separate the opponent's arm, cut the angle, and finish the arm triangle with shoulder pressure rather than arm squeeze.
shortInstruction: Separate the arm, step over the head, drop your weight — the arm triangle from mount is shoulder pressure, not biceps strength.
summary: The arm triangle from mount is one of the highest percentage submissions from the dominant mount position. Unlike the regular arm triangle from side control, the mount version allows you to use your full body weight. The key is separating their arm from their body (usually by driving your forearm into their biceps), stepping over their head, and dropping your chest weight onto their trapped shoulder.
whyItWorks: Mount gives you gravity advantage — your entire body weight compresses their neck and arm.
The arm triangle traps both a carotid artery and their shoulder — two pressure points from one movement.
Once the angle is cut and your shoulder is on their neck, they cannot bridge or roll you off.
Danaher principle: mount arm triangles are the highest percentage mount finish because they combine position and submission.
commonMistakes: Trying to finish without first separating the arm from their body — the arm must be isolated.
Stepping over the head too early — step over only after the arm is pinned to their neck.
Squeezing with the arms instead of driving the shoulder — arm squeeze burns out; shoulder pressure finishes.
Losing mount position to chase the finish — maintain heavy chest pressure throughout.
coachingCues: Separate the arm, then step over — never step before separation.
Shoulder to the neck, not biceps to the neck.
Drop your weight like a deadlift — heavy and controlled.
If they roll, follow their rotation and re-attach.
safetySummary: Apply shoulder pressure gradually — the arm triangle compresses the neck and shoulder simultaneously.
Do not crank the opponent's head to force the arm separation.
Tap early on neck compression — distinguish between choke pressure and neck crank.
keyCorrections: If you can't separate the arm, switch to a crossface or wrist control to break their frame.
If they bridge you off, your base is too narrow — widen your knees and lower your hips.
If they roll to escape, follow their rotation and take the back.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Mount position: separate their arm with forearm or wrist control → guide their arm to their neck → step over their head → drop chest weight → finish.

decisionTree.condition: they defend the arm triangle by hiding the arm
decisionTree.action: switch to mounted armbar or S-mount attacks.
The arm triangle from mount chains directly to the back take if they roll to escape.

moneyDetails: Separate their arm by driving your forearm into their triceps, pushing it toward their head — not away from their body.
Once the arm is against their neck, step your nearside leg over their head — this locks the position.
Drop your chest weight onto your own shoulder — the pressure transfers through your shoulder to their neck.
If they bridge, lower your hips and spread your weight — you want to be 'heavy,' not high.
nextStep: After the arm triangle from mount, learn the mounted triangle and S-mount armbar.
fixItFast: Arm keeps slipping? Pin it against your own chest before stepping over.
They bridge you off? Widen your knees and drop your hips closer to the mat.
Can't finish? Your angle is too square — cut a sharper angle toward their head.
